title: Consistency Models
description: Navigate the spectrum of consistency models — from strict and sequential to causal, eventual, read-your-writes, and monotonic reads.

segments.text: The CAP theorem tells us we can't have everything. But 'consistency' isn't just one thing — it's a spectrum. Today we'll walk through the major consistency models from strongest to weakest, and see what each one actually guarantees.

Strict consistency means every read returns the most recent write, globally, instantly. As if there's a single copy of the data that everyone accesses simultaneously. In a distributed system, this requires perfectly synchronized clocks — which is physically impossible.

Sequential consistency relaxes things slightly. All operations appear in some global order, and each client's operations appear in the order they were issued. You might not see the latest value instantly, but you'll never see operations out of order.

Causal consistency only orders operations that are causally related. If I post a message and you reply to it, everyone must see my message before your reply. But unrelated operations can appear in different orders on different nodes.
segments.thought_prompt: Can you think of a scenario where causal consistency would break the user experience?

segments.text: Eventual consistency is the weakest common model. It only guarantees that if no new writes occur, all replicas will eventually converge to the same value. How long 'eventually' takes is unspecified. It could be milliseconds or minutes.

With eventual consistency, you might update your profile picture and then immediately see the old picture on a refresh. Or add an item to your cart but not see it when you go to checkout. These anomalies are real and frustrating for users.

Read-your-writes consistency is a practical middle ground. It guarantees that after you write a value, you will always see that value on subsequent reads. Other users might see stale data, but you never see your own writes disappear.

Monotonic reads guarantee that if you've seen a value at time T, you'll never see an older value on subsequent reads. Time doesn't go backward for you. Without this, refreshing a page could show you increasingly older data.
segments.thought_prompt: How would you implement read-your-writes if your database has multiple replicas?

segments.text: In practice, read-your-writes is often implemented by routing a user's reads to the same replica that handled their writes. Or by tracking a version number and ensuring reads return at least that version. Sticky sessions can help too.

Stronger consistency means more coordination, more latency, and less availability. Weaker consistency means faster operations but more potential for stale reads. Most real systems mix models: strong consistency for financial data, eventual for social feeds.

Understanding these models is crucial because when someone says 'consistent,' you need to ask: which kind? The answer shapes your architecture, your performance, and your user experience. Next, we'll look at vector clocks — the mechanism that makes causal consistency possible.
